summary: Defines DHCPv6 options for passing a list of available recursive DNS name servers and a domain search list to a client. This lets a host learn which servers to ask for name lookups, without manual setup. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A new computer needs to know whom to ask for directions to a website. This lets the network hand it a short list of helpers, so it does not have to be told by hand.

questions: how does dhcpv6 provide dns servers
how does a client get dns servers from dhcpv6
what is a domain search list
subtitle: Two DHCPv6 options that tell a client which DNS servers to ask and which domains to search.

tldr.problem: A host using DHCPv6 needs to learn which DNS recursive name servers to query and which domains to append to short names, without anyone configuring that by hand.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two DHCPv6 options: a DNS Recursive Name Server option (code 23) carrying a list of IPv6 addresses, and a Domain Search List option (code 24) carrying a list of domain names.
tldr.outcome: A client can get its resolver settings from the DHCPv6 server. The RFC warns that a rogue DHCP server could use these options to misdirect lookups, and recommends DHCP authentication.

today: RFC 3646 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the two DHCPv6 DNS options.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3646 describes two options for passing Domain Name Service (DNS) configuration in DHCPv6, the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 defined in RFC 3315. The DNS itself is specified in RFC 1034 and RFC 1035.

Throughout the document, the word DHCP means DHCPv6 unless said otherwise. The acknowledgements note that these options were originally part of the DHCPv6 specification itself.
sections.eli5: When a computer joins a network, it asks a helper for settings. This document adds two new settings the helper can hand out: whom to ask about names, and where to look for them.

sections.title: The DNS Recursive Name Server Option
sections.content:
The DNS Recursive Name Server option gives a client a list of one or more IPv6 addresses of DNS recursive name servers. The client's DNS resolver MAY send its queries to them. The servers are listed in order of preference for use by the client resolver.

The option has an option-code of OPTION_DNS_SERVERS (23) and an option-len that gives the length of the server list in octets. That length must be a multiple of 16, because each server is one 128-bit IPv6 address.
sections.eli5: It is a list of helpers' phone numbers, with the best one first. The computer tries them in that order when it needs to look something up.

sections.title: The Domain Search List Option
sections.content:
The Domain Search List option specifies the domain search list the client is to use when resolving hostnames with DNS. It does not apply to other name resolution mechanisms.

The option has an option-code of OPTION_DOMAIN_LIST (24), an option-len giving the length of the searchlist field in octets, and the searchlist itself. The domain names in the list MUST be encoded as specified in the section on representation and use of domain names in RFC 3315.
sections.eli5: If you type just a short name, the computer tacks on each place from this list to try to find it, like trying a nickname with each family's last name.

sections.title: Where the Options May Appear
sections.content: Each option MUST NOT appear in any message other than these: Solicit, Advertise, Request, Renew, Rebind, Information-Request and Reply. The same list applies to both options.
sections.eli5: There is a short list of message types that are allowed to carry these settings. They must not be stuck onto any other kind of message.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An intruder DHCP server could use the DNS Recursive Name Server option to make clients send queries to an intruder DNS recursive name server, whose answers may be used to spoof DNS names. To avoid this, the client SHOULD require DHCP authentication (see RFC 3315) before installing a list of servers.

An intruder could also use the Domain Search List option to make clients search invalid domains for incompletely specified names. The RFC notes that DNSSEC support does not avert this attack, because the records in the invalid domains may be legitimately signed. How exposed a host is depends partly on its resolver; RFC 1535 and section 6 of RFC 1536 discuss searchlist weaknesses.

  • Hosts implementing the domain search option SHOULD also implement the searchlist recommendations of RFC 1536, section 6.
  • Manually configured DNS parameters SHOULD NOT be overridden by DHCP.
  • A host SHOULD require DHCP authentication before accepting a domain search option.
sections.eli5: If a trickster pretends to be the helper, they could send your computer to the wrong places. So the computer should check that the helper really is who it says it is.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA assigned option code 23 to the DNS Recursive Name Server option and option code 24 to the Domain Search List option, from the DHCP option code space defined in RFC 3315.
sections.eli5: Each new setting needs its own number so everyone agrees what it means. These two got 23 and 24.
